passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Avni, Wednesday.
During the letter-writing task, Avni erased the word "Dear" so many times that the page tore. She started again. By the end of the period, she had written only two lines and would not hand them in. "It's messy. It's all wrong."
When Irawati said, "Mine has mistakes too," Avni just shook her head and began to cry.
I knelt beside her and showed her my own lesson plan, full of crossings-out. "Mistakes are how we find out what to learn next."
What I'll do next: tomorrow I'll give the class "pencil-only drafts" with no erasers allowed, and I'll ask Avni to circle one mistake she's proud of finding.

qa.q: What did Avni erase so many times that the page tore?
qa.a: The word "Dear".

qa.q: How did Avni feel about her two lines, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt upset and ashamed of any flaw, calling it "messy" and "all wrong", refusing to hand it in and crying.

qa.q: How does the teacher's plan help Avni see mistakes differently?
qa.a: No-eraser drafts and circling a mistake she is proud of finding turn errors into a normal part of learning instead of failure.

qa.q: What might Irawati have been hoping for when she said "Mine has mistakes too"?
qa.a: Irawati was probably trying to comfort Avni and show her that mistakes are normal, and may have felt a bit helpless when Avni kept crying.

grounding: Shows a teacher noting a child who erases until the paper tears and cries at small errors, and planning ways to show mistakes are part of learning.

passage:
The school bus would come at 7:20, and at 7:05 Yash was still repainting one corner of his volcano model. "The brown is uneven! I can't take it like this."
Hemant looked at the clock, then at his son's shaking hands. Part of him was proud; Yash worked so carefully. Part of him ached.
"Yash, look at me." He crouched down. "Remember my office presentation last month? I spelled the company's name wrong on the first slide. Big letters."
Yash stared. "What happened?"
"Someone pointed it out, I said oops, and we carried on. They still gave us the project."
Yash sniffed.
"Your volcano is good enough. The uneven corner is fine, I promise. And I love how much you care."
At 7:18, they carried it out together, one corner a little uneven.

qa.q: What time was the school bus coming?
What was Hemant feeling as he watched Yash repaint the corner?
qa.a: He felt torn: proud of how carefully Yash worked, but also worried and aching to see him so stressed.

qa.q: What did Hemant do well to ease Yash's stress?
qa.a: He shared his own spelling mistake and how it turned out fine, and said the volcano was good enough without shaming Yash's care.

qa.q: What would change if Hemant had said "Stop being silly"?
qa.a: Yash might feel ashamed of caring so much, and his stress could get worse instead of easing.

grounding: Shows a father torn between pride and worry at his son's stress over tiny errors, sharing his own mistake and showing good enough is fine.

passage:
Last term I got 96 in the chemistry exam. Everyone clapped. I felt nothing. Just: why not 100?
Looking back, that was when studying stopped being fun. Before, I liked chemistry. I used to draw molecules in my notebook for no reason. Then every test became a test of whether I was good enough.
The funny thing is, I didn't even study more. I sat at my desk till midnight, scared to start, scrolling and tidying. Then I'd cram in panic at two a.m.
Arohi asked me once, "Aren't you happy with 96?" I said, "It was a lucky paper." She looked at me like I was a stranger.
I'm trying something now. When I get a mark, I write one thing I enjoyed learning before I let myself look at the number.
Ujjwal

qa.q: What mark did Ujjwal get in the chemistry exam?
How did Ujjwal feel after getting 96, and why?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt empty, feeling nothing but "why not 100?", because the standard kept moving higher.

qa.q: What is Ujjwal trying now, and why might it help?
qa.a: Writing one thing Ujjwal enjoyed learning before looking at the mark, which may bring back some joy and loosen the grip of the number.

qa.q: How might Arohi have felt when Ujjwal called it "a lucky paper"?
qa.a: Arohi seemed surprised and a bit worried, looking at Ujjwal like a stranger, since a 96 seemed worth being happy about.

grounding: Shows a teen whose rising standards bring late-night dread, procrastination and emptiness after a good result, with joy draining from learning.

passage:
Results were pinned up outside the staff room in their Jaipur school. Kishore was first again, 98.5 per cent. Madhav was fifteenth and fine with it.
But Kishore wasn't celebrating. He was staring at the physics column, lips moving. "I lost one mark on a unit. One mark."
Some boys behind them muttered, "Topper's crying over 99, poor thing." Madhav felt a flash of annoyance at them, and something else at Kishore's face: worry.
He waited until the others left. "Hey. You did amazing. Seriously."
Kishore shrugged. "It should've been full."
"Want to come to the cricket ground after school? No studying allowed."
Kishore hesitated. "I have to redo that chapter."
"One hour. Then redo it."
After a moment, Kishore half-smiled. "One hour."

qa.q: What percentage did Kishore get?
qa.a: 98.5 per cent.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling as he watched Kishore's face?
qa.a: Madhav felt annoyed at the boys who mocked Kishore, and worried about how anxious Kishore looked over one mark.

qa.q: Which of Madhav's choices could make Kishore feel less alone?
qa.a: Praising him sincerely instead of joining the mocking, and inviting him to the cricket ground for an hour with no studying.

qa.q: What might it be like for Kishore to hear "Topper's crying over 99"?
qa.a: It may make Kishore feel lonely and misunderstood, since others see only his success and not how anxious he is.

grounding: Shows a classmate noticing a topper who cannot enjoy results, choosing kindness over mocking and inviting him to relax.

passage:
The job portal on Arohi's laptop had been open for three weeks in their Chennai flat. Eleven saved listings. Zero applications.
"Did you send the design one?" Keerthana asked, dropping her bag.
"Not yet. My portfolio's not ready. The second project looks amateur."
"You've been saying that since March."
Arohi pulled her knees up. "If I send something average, they'll think I'm average. Then what's the point?"
"So it's perfect or nothing?"
"...Kind of."
Keerthana sat beside her and scrolled through the portfolio. "This is good. Not flawless. Good."
Arohi stared at the screen. The deadline for the design listing was midnight. Her cursor hovered over "Apply," then moved back to "Edit portfolio" again. She sighed, feeling stuck and tired of herself.

qa.q: How many listings had Arohi saved?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How does Arohi feel as her cursor moves back to "Edit portfolio"?
qa.a: She feels stuck and tired of herself, afraid that sending anything average means she is average.

qa.q: What small step could help Arohi get unstuck?
qa.a: She could send the design application tonight with the portfolio as it is, since Keerthana says it is good, and improve the second project later.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see Arohi's delay?
qa.a: Keerthana sees a good portfolio being held back since March and seems concerned, gently naming the perfect-or-nothing thinking.

grounding: Shows a young adult delaying job applications because her work may not be flawless, caught in all-or-nothing thinking.

passage:
Vandana set a timer on her phone for forty minutes and wrote at the top of a page: ROUGH DRAFT, ALLOWED TO BE BAD.
Last semester she'd rewritten the first paragraph of her sociology paper nine times and missed the deadline. This time, in the Delhi university library, she kept going even when sentences felt clumsy.
When the timer rang, she had three ugly pages. Tarun, across the table, raised an eyebrow. "Done already?"
"Done with the rough one." She asked herself the question the counsellor had suggested: what if this is ninety percent as good as perfect? Would anyone fail me? Probably not.
She edited for one hour and submitted two days early. Her chest still felt tight when she clicked Submit.
That evening she booked another session with the college counsellor to keep working on the worry, which hadn't fully gone away.

qa.q: How long was Vandana's timer set for?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel when she clicked Submit?
qa.a: She still felt anxious, with a tight chest, even though she had finished early.

qa.q: Which strategies helped Vandana finish this time?
qa.a: A time limit, a rough draft allowed to be bad, and asking what would happen if the work were ninety percent as good.

qa.q: How might Tarun see Vandana's quick rough draft?
qa.a: Tarun was surprised she was done so fast, perhaps not knowing the rough draft was a deliberate step to beat perfectionism.

grounding: Shows a young adult using a time limit, a rough first version and a good-enough question, and seeking counselling for lingering anxiety.

passage:
Team lead's note, Devika, quarterly check-in.
Devika's reports are the best on the team. Clients trust her work. But this quarter I've seen the cost.
She rechecked every one of Hafsa's spreadsheets line by line, then redid two of them herself at midnight. Hafsa told me she feels "like a child" and has stopped suggesting ideas. In our weekly meeting Devika said, "If it's not perfect, it's not done," and the room went quiet.
She also said to me, almost in passing, "I can't remember my last weekend off. I'm so tired I snap at everyone, including myself."
What I did next: we agreed Hafsa owns the supplier report fully, with one review from Devika, not five. I asked Devika to take this Friday off, and suggested she look at the employee support line if the exhaustion doesn't ease. We'll meet again in two weeks.

qa.q: What did Devika say in the weekly meeting?
qa.a: "If it's not perfect, it's not done."

qa.q: How is Devika feeling this quarter?
qa.a: She feels exhausted and irritable, so tired that she snaps at everyone, including herself.

qa.q: What steps did the team lead take to reduce the cost of Devika's perfectionism?
qa.a: Giving Hafsa full ownership of the supplier report with one review, asking Devika to take Friday off, and pointing to the support line if exhaustion continues.

qa.q: How has Devika's rechecking affected Hafsa?
qa.a: Hafsa feels "like a child" and has stopped suggesting ideas, so the strain shows in their working relationship.

grounding: Shows a team lead noting a professional whose harsh rechecking and refusal to delegate bring excellent work but also burnout and strained relationships.

passage:
In the courtyard of their Istanbul apartment block, Selin had drawn the hopscotch squares herself, perfectly straight. "You have to hop on your left foot on seven. That's the rule."
Hana skipped seven. "Let's make it more fun. We can jump anywhere!"
Selin's face crumpled. "No! Then it's not the game!" She stamped off and sat on the steps, arms tight around her knees.
Her mother had noticed that since the moving boxes appeared in the hall, Selin had been making more rules for everything.
Later, her mother suggested something. "Every game starts the same way: you both say the rules out loud first. And at the end, you can each choose one new rule for next time."
The next day, Selin said the rules. Then, a little nervously, she let Hana add one: "Clap on number ten."

qa.q: Which foot did Selin's rule say to hop on at seven?
qa.a: The left foot.

qa.q: How did Selin feel when Hana changed the rules?
qa.a: She felt upset and unsettled; her face crumpled, she stamped off and hugged her knees on the steps.

qa.q: Why might her mother's idea help Selin loosen her rules?
qa.a: Saying the rules at the start and adding one new rule at the end gives a calm, predictable structure, so change feels safer.

qa.q: How might Hana see Selin's strict rules?
qa.a: Hana just wanted to make the game more fun, so she may feel confused or bossed about when Selin gets so upset.

grounding: Shows a child who insists on fixed game rules when her world feels uncertain, and how a calm, predictable structure helps loosen them.

passage:
Divyansh, you want everyone's trip to go your way, na? Your Bidisha Pishi was the same at sixteen. Let me tell you.
For our class picnic, I made the whole plan: the bus times, the menu, who sat where. When Tapas suggested the riverbank instead of the fort, I said, "No, I've already decided." When Mitali packed the sandwiches, I re-wrapped every one because she'd done it "wrong".
My stomach was in knots the whole week. What if the bus was late? What if it rained? If I wasn't in charge, it felt like everything would fall apart.
On the picnic day, Mitali sat with other girls and wouldn't talk to me. That night she said, "You never listen to anyone." That hurt, because she was right.
The next outing, I chose one thing to plan, the games. The rest, I let others decide. It was scary. And it was the best picnic we had.

qa.q: What did Tapas suggest instead of the fort?
qa.a: The riverbank.

qa.q: What was young Bidisha feeling during the week before the picnic?
qa.a: She felt anxious, with her stomach in knots, afraid everything would fall apart if she wasn't in charge.

qa.q: What choice did young Bidisha make for the next outing, and why did it help?
qa.a: She planned only the games and let others decide the rest, which made space for friends to be heard and led to the best picnic.

qa.q: How did Mitali feel about the re-wrapped sandwiches and the plans?
qa.a: Mitali felt unheard and hurt, saying, "You never listen to anyone," and sat with other girls on the picnic day.

grounding: Shows an aunt recalling how, as a teen, fear of things going wrong made her control every plan until a friend felt unheard, and how she let go a little.

passage:
In a cafe near the university in Buenos Aires, Layla had the group project spreadsheet open and was colour-coding it again. "Valentina, you'll do the survey by Tuesday. Actually, send it to me first, I'll check it."
"I've done surveys before," Valentina said.
"I know. I just like to be sure." Layla's knee was bouncing under the table. Last year one group member had vanished before a deadline, and she'd stayed up two nights fixing everything.
Valentina put her cup down. "Layla, you check everything. It's like you think we'll ruin it."
Layla felt her face go hot. Under the bossiness was fear, cold and familiar. "I'm scared it'll fall apart," she admitted.
"So try trusting me with one thing. Just the survey. No checking."
Layla breathed out. "Okay. Just the survey."
On Tuesday, the survey arrived. It was good.

qa.q: What was Valentina given to do by Tuesday?
qa.a: The survey.

qa.q: What was Layla feeling beneath the checking?
qa.a: She was scared the project would fall apart, a cold, familiar fear from last year, shown by her bouncing knee.

qa.q: What small step helped Layla practise trust?
qa.a: Agreeing to let Valentina do the survey with no checking, which ended with a good result on Tuesday.

qa.q: How does Valentina experience Layla's constant checking?
qa.a: Valentina feels doubted, as if Layla thinks the group will ruin the project, even though she has done surveys before.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose micromanaging hides a fear of losing safety, and who practises trusting a partner with one small task.
